item.title: Canonical web services get stage fright ahead of Ubuntu Summit
item.description: A swathe of Canonical's web services has been offline for hours, an awkward warm-up for tomorrow's Ubuntu Summit. Canonical's status page lists widespread disruption beginning at approximately 1100 UTC, affecting gopkg.in, Ubuntu cloud images and mailing lists, jaas.ai, the Ubuntu keyserver, Launchpad PPAs, the Livepatch API, canonical.com, Ubuntu login, maas.io, and 16 other services. Landscape is also affected. Email and the company's Discourse forums remain available. The Register has asked Canonical for more information but had received no response at publication time. The company suffered a DDoS attack last month , although the cause of this outage has not been confirmed. The timing is unfortunate. As the banner across the top of the Discourse forum page says: "The Ubuntu Summit starts tomorrow – join from anywhere!" The online event runs on November 12-13. For the first time since the 2022 Summit in Prague, The Reg FOSS desk won't be attending in person. Canonical is still experimenting with the format of the event, and the last few have been primarily online, with just a small in-person audience in its London offices. This is the second of two Summits this year, labeled 26.04 and 26.10 to mirror Ubuntu's release cycle. The timetable , hosted on the Discourse site, lists several talks on AI and agentic coding. The AI-heavy program we reported from June's event appears to be continuing. ®

item.title: 'There's tremendous demand': Rocket Lab raises price of Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million
item.description: null The coming launch bottleneck has ramped up demand for a rocket that has yet to leave the ground. Rocket Lab announced on Monday (Nov. 9) that it recently raised the price of a Neutron launch from $55 million to $70 million — an increase of more than 25%, for a ride on a rocket that's set to debut in 2027. "Launch is extremely constrained, and that is exactly the situation we predicted," Rocket Lab founder and CEO Peter Beck said on Monday during the company's third-quarter earnings call. "We saw a pent-up launch market on the horizon, and rather than provide early discounted launches, we set out to deliver a rocket into an environment with extreme demand at full price or higher." Rocket Lab is best known for Electron , a workhorse small-satellite launcher that debuted in 2017 and now has 90 orbital missions under its belt. The 59-foot-tall (18 meters) expendable rocket and can haul 660 pounds (300 kilograms) to low Earth orbit (LEO). Neutron is the company's entry into the medium-lift market. It features a reusable first stage, stands 141 feet (43 m) tall and can carry 14.3 tons (13 metric tons) of payload to LEO. Rocket Lab announced Neutron back in 2021 and first targeted a 2024 debut for the vehicle. But various problems have cropped up over the years, pushing things back. Last month, for example, Rocket Lab announced that it was delaying the first Neutron flight from late 2026 into 2027 due to a manufacturing issue (which it says is now under control). Such setbacks have not dampened demand for Neutron's services, however. During Monday's call, Beck revealed that Rocket Lab booked eight Neutron launches during the third quarter of 2026, which ran from July 1 through Sept. 30. The contracts for those eight flights are worth "a total of roughly 515 million, including multiple missions on a new escalated base price of $70 million," Beck said. Neutron's first 16 launches are now sold out, he added, and bookings from here on will be for flights in the 2030s. "The demand is a function of both a tightening global launch supply and our customers' confidence that Rocket Lab is the right partner to break the world's launch bottleneck," Beck said. Artist's illustration of Neutron's first stage coming down for a landing on a ship at sea. (Image credit: Rocket Lab) That bottleneck is coming in 2028 or so, when SpaceX plans to retire its Falcon 9 rocket . For some perspective, and comparison with Neutron: SpaceX currently charges $74 million for each Falcon 9 launch. The rocket has a reusable first stage and can carry about 25 tons (22.7 metric tons) to LEO. The medium lifter has been the world's most prolific rocket for the past few years. In 2025, for example, it flew 165 times — roughly the same number of orbital missions as all other launchers in the world combined. And all 165 of those flights were successful. But SpaceX is phasing out the Falcon 9 — and its heavy-lift cousin, the Falcon Heavy — nonetheless, shifting all launch work over to its f

item.title: Russia’s Central Bank Clears Exchange to Open Bitcoin and Crypto Trading on Nov. 22
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Russia’s Central Bank Clears Exchange to Open Bitcoin and Crypto Trading on Nov. 22 The Bank of Russia said Wednesday that exchanges may start organized trading in cryptocurrencies on Nov. 22, once the central bank has approved their trading rules, a step that lands just ahead of Moscow Exchange’s planned Dec. 1 bitcoin launch. The ordinance, which amends the Bank of Russia’s rules for organized trading, was registered by the Justice Ministry on Nov. 3 and published Wednesday on the regulator’s site. It takes effect 10 days after publication, on Nov. 22. Exchanges will have to register the brokers, trust managers and central counterparties that take part in crypto trades, keep registers of orders and deals, and monitor the activity. They must also calculate a current price, a weighted-average price, a market price and a closing price, and report trading activity to the central bank in the same way they already do for other assets. The regulator was clear about the order of operations. Exchanges may open crypto markets from Nov. 22, it said, “but first they must agree with the regulator on the rules for conducting such trading.” It did not say whether any venue has already cleared that review. Who can buy, and what they can buy A separate ordinance, published Nov. 6 and due to take effect Nov. 17, sets the menu for ordinary buyers. The Bank of Russia approved bitcoin, ether and Tether’s USDT for purchase by non-qualified investors, and said exchanges may admit those assets to public trading from that date. Non-qualified investors can buy through a broker, a trust manager or a registered crypto exchange office, on an exchange or over the counter. Purchases through a single intermediary may not exceed 300,000 rubles a year, roughly $3,600 at the official exchange rate. Qualified investors can access all cryptoassets with no purchase cap. Both groups still have to pass a knowledge test and read a risk disclosure before they can trade. The list is limited to the most liquid assets that meet the law’s tests for market capitalization, average daily volume and at least five years of pricing history on foreign exchanges. Moscow Exchange still aims for Dec. 1 Moscow Exchange, Russia’s largest trading venue, announced on Nov. 2 that it plans to offer bitcoin, ether and USDT trades from Dec. 1, initially as a pilot while participants connect. Trading would run on its existing stock-market systems from 6:50 a.m. to 11:50 p.m. Moscow time, with the National Clearing Centre clearing the deals and clients able to settle the same day or the next. Bitcoin Magazine reported the Dec. 1 plan last week, including the U.S. sanctions that already cover the exchange and its clearing house. Boris Blokhin, a senior managing director at the exchange, said in early October that Moscow Exchange would not need additional licenses to start and would use a partner settlement digital depository. item.title: ICE and OKX Set Nov. 23 Tokenized Stock Launch After 67 Companies Opt Out
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine ICE and OKX Set Nov. 23 Tokenized Stock Launch After 67 Companies Opt Out OKX and New York Stock Exchange parent Intercontinental Exchange (ICE) will open their tokenized stock venue on Nov. 23, the companies said Wednesday, offering more than 70 assets under a temporary SEC exemption even as 67 companies, including Apple, Tesla and Meta, have already objected. The OKX announcement said more than 70 assets are expected to be listed, including securities from Better.com, BitGo, Circle, Coinbase, Robinhood, Securitize and Strategy (MSTR), as well as 59 exchange-traded funds from Direxion. Strategy will also list its preferred stocks, such as STRC. Access at launch is limited to eligible U.S. customers of OKX Inc. who have activated a CeDeFi Wallet, passed identity checks and completed onboarding with the joint venture, which is called OKXICE and is owned equally by ICE and OKC USA Holding Inc., an OKX affiliate. Trading will run around the clock in the OKX app. “The future of finance is onchain, and we have an opportunity to build it here in America, with the standards, safeguards and ambition that investors expect,” said former New York Gov. Andrew Cuomo, who co-chairs OKXICE with Trabue Bland. The companies did not say how many of the more than 70 assets will trade on the first day, or how much liquidity the pools will have at the open. The venue is not a registered exchange or broker-dealer and is not approved by the SEC, the announcement said. How the venue will work Trading will run through automated market maker pools built on Uniswap v4 and deployed on X Layer, the Ethereum layer-2 network OKX operates. Only approved wallets can trade or add liquidity. Securitize will provide the tokenization infrastructure. Each token represents a security entitlement backed one-for-one by a U.S. share held by a registered broker-dealer, and holders keep the usual shareholder rights, including dividends, voting and corporate actions, the venue said in a Nov. 5 public notice required under the exemption. Customers will hold the tokens in their own wallets. OKXICE will not hold the assets or the private keys. The tokens will be paired with payment stablecoins such as USDC and USDG. The venue does not operate an order book, does not extend credit and does not conduct primary offerings, the notice said. 67 companies have already opted out The same Nov. 5 notice lists 67 issuers that had sent a written objection by that date, among them Apple, Amazon, Tesla, Meta, Netflix, Nvidia, Microsoft, JPMorgan, Goldman Sachs, Costco, Nike and Home Depot. The list has grown from 50 objectors in an Oct. 30 notice. The objections stem from the SEC’s five-year “Innovation Exemption,” issued Sept. 17, which lets tokenized securities venues trade blockchain versions of U.S. stocks through automated market makers without registering as exchanges. item.title: Apple's touchscreen MacBook Pro does not like to be taken apart
item.description: Apple's first touchscreen MacBook got a mixed reception from iFixit's teardown specialists, who praised its easily replaced lid but found fans and USB-C ports buried beneath the logic board. The MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display was unveiled at the end of October. It features a tandem OLED screen that stacks two layers of organic light-emitting pixels, eliminating the need for a backlight, and adds touch capability to the MacBook line for the first time. Although the vendor was patted on the back in recent years for improving the repairability of its famously locked-down products, this machine shows Apple still has some way to go. The good? The entire lid comes off relatively easily. Its three-screw hinges closely resemble those on the M6 14-inch MacBook Pro, while streamlined display cable brackets simplify removal. Apple's Repair Assistant tool also handled a full system board swap well. Despite concerns about Touch ID fingerprint authentication, everything went relatively smoothly when iFixit paired a touchscreen from one machine with a logic board from another. On the first boot, Repair Assistant recognized the battery, display, and Touch ID sensor, and touch control needed no separate calibration. The bad? Replacing the panel alone is not possible. When iFixit tried to separate it from the lid, the glass delaminated, cracking the OLED and touch-sensitive layers beneath. That could make for a costlier repair than bargained for. Under the bottom cover, the PROLED has a similar internal layout to the last few models of MacBook Pros, with the fans, board, speakers, and trackpad all in the same places. That means the same annoyances persist. The MagSafe power connector can be removed via two screws and a bracket, yet the USB-C ports can't be extracted the same way because the logic board is in the way. The headphone jack and the fans also require removing the system board first, and the HDMI port and SDXC card reader are soldered to the board itself, as is the storage and memory. Another gripe is that this MacBook's battery pack is hard to remove, though at least it is removable, unlike in many thin-and-light laptops. The tested Pro weighs 1.38 kg or about 3 pounds. For these reasons, the MacBook Pro with PROLED XDR display earns a 5 out of 10 repairability score from iFixit , but this is actually a one point increase over the score it gave the M5 MacBook Pro. The Apple logo has its own lighting. Older MacBooks with illuminated logos borrowed light from the LCD backlight shining through an apple-shaped window in the lid. This model uses a strip of LEDs along one edge of the logo, passing through a diffuser for an even glow. Because it sits behind the display panel, it would be nearly impossible to repair if it failed, especially if the panel is destroyed during removal. Under a microscope, the PROLED XDR display looks very different from earlier MacBooks: the blue subpixel is significantly larger than the green and red ones. The reason, we're t

item.title: Trump wanted little Kei trucks for America, Toyota makes it happen
item.description: The idea that Americans should be offered a greater choice of smaller cars has support from strange bedfellows indeed. After all, who could forget President Trump—usually one to take a maximalist approach to any problem— announcing last year that he wanted the Department of Transportation to make Japan’s diminutive “Kei” cars legal here in the US. Ars’ attempts to get DoT to tell us more about the potential influx of little vehicles have mostly fallen on deaf ears. But this week, there has been movement on the topic, with Toyota announcing that it will bring back the Scion brand with the KEI-01. What’s a Kei car? In the US, the preponderance of humongous SUVs is a consequence largely of government policies, specifically corporate average fuel economy standards that made it less profitable to sell smaller, efficient cars. Japan’s Kei cars are what happens if the government instead restricts the size, engine capacity, and power output. Read full article Comments

item.title: Hubble Space Telescope reveals glittering stars with mysterious origins | Space photo of the day for Nov. 11, 2026
item.description: null The Hubble Space Telescope has captured a breathtaking view of thousands of stars glittering like cosmic jewels in a dazzling display of blue, gold and orange. But this spectacular scene is far more than just a pretty picture. Some of these stars are almost as old as the universe itself and could hold clues to how our Milky Way formed. M30 is a globular star cluster located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth. (Image credit: ESA/Hubble & NASA, M. Libralato, G. Piotto, A. Sarajedini) What is it? The exquisite image released by ESA on Nov. 5 shows Messier 30 (M30), a densely packed collection of stars located approximately 27,500 light-years from Earth in the constellation Capricornus. M30 is a globular cluster, a roughly spherical collection of tens of thousands to millions of stars held together by gravity . Our Milky Way is home to at least 150 of these ancient stellar gatherings, some of which are estimated to be between 11.5 billion and 13.5 billion years old. For comparison, the universe itself is approximately 13.8 billion years old! Why is it amazing Besides looking like a vast cosmic treasure trove glittering across the universe, M30 also has a fascinating story to tell. Globular clusters are essentially cosmic time capsules. Their ancient stars preserve chemical clues about the conditions that existed when they formed, helping astronomers piece together the Milky Way's early history. Astronomers have also discovered that M30, along with several other globular clusters, traverses the Milky Way in the opposite direction to the galaxy's rotation. This unusual motion raises the intriguing possibility that M30 may not have formed in our galaxy at all. It could have simply been captured by the Milky Way billions of years ago.

item.title: Microsoft's Patch Tuesday can't break stuff if it won't install
item.description: Users are having difficulty installing Microsoft's latest Windows patch. Patch Tuesday contained a truckload of fixes for Microsoft products . However, for some users, installing the update, KB5132061, is proving challenging. In the hours after the patch was released, multiple complaints began to surface that the download and installation were failing, with some customers reporting a 0x800F0993 error code. Others say they received a 0x800F0989 error. Microsoft does not currently list any known issues with the update and is yet to make a statement or provide explanation for the glitch. In addition to the security fixes, this patch resolves a number of known issues from previous updates, including a problem where USB Audio 1.0 devices might fail to start and display an error code 10 in Device Manager. In the absence of a statement from Microsoft, several users have taken to sleuthing. One, with the handle of Forceflow on the ElevenForum site, suggested the bug might be related to Windows Sandbox, and said that after disabling the feature and rebooting, the patch installed successfully. However, others reported problems regardless of Windows Sandbox status, and alternative solutions included using DISM (Deployment Image Servicing and Management) to check the package or downloading the update manually. It's an important patch to install, since it addresses 726 vulnerabilities in Windows alone, and the difficulties affected users face are less than ideal. Microsoft patches have lately displayed more gremlins than usual. Out-of-band releases are depressingly regular after updates break functionality. A September Out-of-band release, for example, was hurriedly pushed out after the September 2026 Windows security update caused trouble for Remote Desktop Services. The October Patch Tuesday for Windows Server sent Exchange Servers toppling , with a registry edit workaround suggested. There was no out-of-band update - Microsoft said the problem had been resolved in the November update. At least this latest release appears to be failing before users get a chance to see what is broken this time. ® Updated to add on November 12: Microsoft has confirmed that there was indeed a problem with installing the update for some users, but the good news is that a fix is rolling out and no action is required on the part of customers (at least those connected to the internet and using Windows Update). The bad news is, alas, there appear to be a few issues with the update around printing and activation. Microsoft giveth, and Microsoft taketh away.

item.title: Deutsche Bank Switches On Bitcoin Custody for Paying Clients
item.description: Bitcoin Magazine Deutsche Bank Switches On Bitcoin Custody for Paying Clients Deutsche Bank has switched on its digital asset custody service for paying clients, the German lender said Wednesday, letting institutions and corporations in Europe hold bitcoin with the country’s largest bank less than two months after it first unveiled the plan. The bank announced the service on Sept. 16, saying it would go live with first clients this year once regulators signed off. It now supports bitcoin and ether, along with the USDC, EURC and EURAU stablecoins, according to its product page . Under the setup, Deutsche Bank manages the wallets and private keys on behalf of clients, who can store the assets and transfer them to third parties. The bank pitched that as a way for clients to skip building and maintaining their own custody infrastructure. “In the medium term we aim to deliver a fully integrated, regulated ecosystem that supports the custody, tokenisation, and settlement of digital assets,” said Paul Maley, global head of trust and securities services at Deutsche Bank. The bank did not name its first clients, say how many have signed up or disclose what it charges to hold the coins. The service is aimed at institutional and corporate clients, not retail customers. What Deutsche Bank is offering The product page describes private keys stored in hardware security modules, a choice of warm and cold storage, multi-factor authentication, segregation of client assets and a customizable approval process for client transfers. Clients reach the service through Autobahn, Deutsche Bank’s multi-channel gateway, or its Corporate Bank portal. The service is booked out of Deutsche Bank AG in Frankfurt and is available in Germany, with cross-border servicing across Europe through passporting. The bank lists institutional investors, multinationals and corporates, governments and sovereigns, and wealth managers as target clients, and it describes the offering as compliant with the European Union’s MiCA crypto rules. For now the menu is narrow. Deutsche lists custody, transfers and internal moves between warm and cold storage as its initial services, with “further capabilities planned.” The September release said the asset list may grow with client demand and that tokenized financial instruments are on the roadmap. It also carried a warning familiar to anyone in bitcoin: crypto assets held this way are not covered by a deposit-guarantee scheme like the one that protects eligible bank deposits. A tie-up with Deutsche Asset Management Alongside the launch, Deutsche Bank signed a memorandum of understanding with Deutsche Asset Management, the money manager it mostly owns that was known until recently as DWS. The agreement is meant “to explore comprehensive commercial and technical collaboration opportunities in the digital asset space,” the bank said. item.title: NASA asks Earthlings to wave as Voyager 1 reaches a light-day away
item.description: Voyager 1 will become the first human-made object to reach one light-day from Earth next week, and NASA wants us to mark the occasion by flashing our lights at the sky. The spacecraft, which suffered a communications hiccup last month, is traveling at approximately 38,000 mph (61,000 kph) and will mark the 50th anniversary of its launch next year. Before then, it has another distance record to set. "Light-day" is a bit snappier than 16,094,799,096 miles (25,902,068,356 kilometers). NASA puts the crossing at 05:16:07 EST (10:16:07 UTC) on Wednesday, November 18. For "Shine Bright for Voyager's Light-Day," participants are invited to flash the mission's three-letter designation – VGR – in Morse code after sunset on November 17, using a flashlight or NASA's website. According to the space agency, this will create "a symbolic wave of golden light encircling the planet after sunset." It is also a nice way to mark the achievement – Voyager 1 is the most distant human-made object from Earth, and its extraordinary longevity remains a testament to the skill of engineers past and present. Not that Voyager 1 will be able to detect any flashlights on Earth. Its cameras were turned off decades ago, after the famous Pale Blue Dot image was captured. NASA has invited the public to join in a spacecraft photo opportunity before. On July 19, 2013, Cassini photographed Earth and the Moon from its orbit around Saturn for "The Day the Earth Smiled," while people back home were encouraged to look up and "just smile at the sheer joy of being alive on a Pale Blue Dot." Voyager 2, the spacecraft's sibling, is not expected to reach the same milestone for another nine years. It took a different path through the solar system to swing past Uranus and Neptune. It will, however, be uncertain as to whether Voyager 2 will still be able to communicate by then – even with recent efforts to eke out the probe's dwindling power supply, margins are razor thin. ®

item.title: Google DeepMind just mathematically verified key parts of Signal
item.description: Google DeepMind researchers used agentic AI to mathematically prove, or “formally verify,” a number of the Signal protocol’s key cryptographic guarantees—a landmark development for the widely used cryptography and AI itself. Conducted as a sort of proof-of-concept project in just four weeks, the work is significant in two ways. It serves as further independent validation of the cryptography that protects massive quantities of the world's communications on platforms like the Signal app , Google Messages, and WhatsApp. And it demonstrates Google DeepMind's formal verification capabilities using a new AI framework called AlphaProof Code. More broadly, AI-aided formal verification is having a moment, but it is unclear how practical it will be for widespread use and how effective it can be at securing large amounts of code. Proponents of formal verification have long referred to it as a sort of holy grail in software security, because it uses math to check and validate that software is functioning as intended—in other words, that it doesn't have critical vulnerabilities. Read full article Comments

item.title: 2013 breach at Russian cybercrime forum resurfaces with millions of victims' credentials
item.description: A 2013 breach of Russian-language cybercrime forum YouHack exposed its members' login details – and millions of credentials they had posted about other victims, according to newly cataloged data. Have I Been Pwned (HIBP) added the breach on Wednesday, recording 7.2 million unique email addresses. Around 107,000 belonged to forum members, whose exposed data included usernames, IP addresses, and mostly unsalted MD5 password hashes. Unsalted MD5 is a poor choice for protecting passwords. It's fast to compute, allowing attackers to test guesses at speed, and identical passwords produce identical hashes. Hardly good hygiene for a hacking forum. You might expect members of a cybercrime forum to know better than to reuse passwords or register with an email address tied to their real identity. Expectations and reality are not always on speaking terms, as AlphaBay founder Alexandre Cazes demonstrated. YouHack, a longtime cybercrime forum, moved to a different domain after the 2013 breach and remains active, giving cybercrims a place to trade stolen credentials and financial data. The data collated from that digital burglary was eventually bundled into 2024's so-called Mother of all Breaches – a 12TB, 26 billion-record mega-dump of files taken from myriad data security lapses. Millions more HIBP separately published its findings concerning another Russian data breach today. It said the 2023 breach of Russian bank Sberbank's loyalty program (SberSpasibo) contained records belonging to 48 million users. The dataset included 3.3 million unique email addresses, alongside phone numbers and dates of birth. Bank card numbers were stored as unsalted SHA-1 hashes, which could let attackers test possible numbers against the leaked hashes for a match. Reporting on the SberSpasibo breach at the time suggested the records were dated between April 2017 and February 2022, and the attack was claimed by the pro-Ukraine hacktivist outfit NLB. NLB also claimed responsibility for an attack on Sberbank's internal systems at the same time, and later took partial credit for an attack on Alfa-Bank , Russia's largest private bank. ®

item.title: Why I recommend the Seestar S30 Plus smart telescope for beginners — full review
item.description: null I’ve used several smart telescopes over the last few years, but I'd recommend the ZWO Seestar S30 Plus to almost anyone wanting to get started in astrophotography. At $499/€499, it’s a complete imaging system that can photograph galaxies, nebulae and star clusters automatically, even from a light-polluted city. Better still, it’s so small that it can live on a bookshelf. The Pleiades (M45), photographed in mosaic mode with the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Andromeda Galaxy (M31) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter The Dumbbell Nebula (M27) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) Jamie Carter I recently captured images of the Dumbbell Nebula (M27), the North America Nebula (NGC 7000), the Andromeda Galaxy (M31) and the Pleiades (M45) with the S30 Plus. All were remarkably easy to capture, and none of the images accompanying this review required external processing. It’s basically point-and-shoot astrophotography — if you live under light-polluted skies, that’s a game-changer. Star trails photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus’s dedicated Star Trail mode. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) I also think the S30 Plus makes an ideal companion to a conventional optical telescope. I can set it to photograph a nebula I have no hope of seeing under light pollution while I try to find brighter objects through the eyepiece of another telescope. It will then get on with collecting photons while I enjoy observing. For anyone who already owns a telescope but doesn’t want the expense and complexity of conventional astrophotography, that’s a compelling proposition. I photographed nebulas despite light pollution The S30 Plus is Seestar’s new entry-level smart telescope. (Image credit: Jamie Carter) (Image credit: Jamie Carter) One problem with buying a cheap optical telescope is that deep-sky objects rarely resemble the colorful photographs you see online. The moon, planets and bright star clusters can look wonderful through an eyepiece, but faint galaxies and nebulas are much harder to appreciate, particularly from a town or city. Like all smart telescopes, the S30 Plus gets around that problem by photographing objects rather than showing them directly. Its camera takes repeated exposures, which the telescope automatically stacks to reduce noise and gradually reveal faint detail. The longer you leave it working, the better the resulting image tends to become. Being able to photograph colorful nebulas without traveling to a remote observing site is one of the biggest attractions of the S30 Plus. For beginners living in cities, it could transform their experience of astronomy. It’s the perfect companion to my optical telescope The North America Nebula (NGC 7000) photographed using the Seestar S30 Plus. item.title: NASA's new UVEX space telescope will peer deep into the universe's most violent events
item.description: null A new NASA space telescope will study the universe in ultraviolet light to reveal the violent and turbulent events that bubble under what appears to be a cosmic sea of tranquility. The Ultraviolet Explorer (UVEX) mission, developed by NASA in conjunction with the California Institute of Technology (Caltech), will be the first mission to create deep all-sky maps in ultraviolet light. Thus, when it launches in 2031, UVEX will join new sky-mapping surveys like NASA's SPHEREx (Spectro-Photometer for the History of the Universe, Epoch of Reionization and Ices Explorer), which scans the cosmos in infrared, and the Vera C. Rubin Observatory, which does the same over the southern hemisphere in visible light, in creating deep-sky maps across a broad swathe of the electromagnetic spectrum. UVEX's ultraviolet views will reveal explosive events such as the collisions between ultra-dense stellar corpses called neutron stars and the supernova explosions that mark the deaths of massive stars and the births of neutron stars and black holes. Additionally, the NASA ultraviolet telescope should be able to detect a multitude of low-mass galaxies much closer to the Milky Way than similar galaxies that are currently being observed millions and even billions of light-years away by NASA's James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) . The $590 million UVEX mission will "advance fundamental frontiers in astrophysics, from understanding the smallest galaxies to diagnosing the aftermath of neutron-star mergers and other cosmic explosions," the mission's principal investigator, Caltech physics professor Fiona Harrison, said in an Oct. 27 statement . "The first major ultraviolet space mission in two decades, UVEX is a bold leap forward in our exploration of the ultraviolet universe," Caltech President Ray Jayawardhana said in the same statement. UVEX will paint a picture of cosmic life, death and afterlife UVEX will benefit from a major leap forward in UV sensitivity thanks to its Caltech-built sensors, which are based on complementary metal–oxide–semiconductor (CMOS) imaging technology. This will help the spacecraft tap into what Harrison described as "the untapped opportunity in the UV." UVEX will be uniquely poised to spot millions of nearby, small, and faint galaxies that are teeming with infant stars that emit bright UV light. "In optical light, it's very hard to distinguish these nearby galaxies from faraway ones that look similar," Harrison said. "UV light will make them easier to find." UVEX won't just be investigating the infancy of stars , however. It will also examine the deaths of ancient stars in the form of supernovas. The supernova relic Pa 30, as seen by the Gemini north telescope. (Image credit: International Gemini Observatory/NOIRLab/NSF/AURA) Supernovas occur when a massive star runs out of fuel for nuclear fusion and can no longer support itself against the inward push of its own gravity. As the core of the star collapses, its outer layers are blasted outward

item.title: Apple tells its Support Community to STFU
item.description: Apple has abruptly stopped accepting new posts on its Support Community, putting the forum into read-only mode ahead of permanent closure on November 20, 2026. Users seeking help with their gizmos from other Apple customers were greeted with the message : "The Apple Support Community will permanently close on November 20, 2026. Starting today, the site will no longer accept new posts and is available in a read-only state. "We want to thank the community members who have contributed their time and expertise to help others with their Apple products." Need help? Head to the official Apple Support site. Want to see if your fellow Apple users have an answer to what ails your device? This is no longer the forum for you. Some reports date the site's origins to 1998, when Apple was busy killing off the Newton platform and launching Mac OS 8.5. Technology has come a long way since then, and recent AI developments have made user-to-user forums like Apple's Support Community less popular. Other places to seek advice remain, and useful answers were never guaranteed. As one user put it on X : "rip to every thread that ended with 'same problem here' and zero solutions." Still, it's an abrupt end to almost three decades of accumulated advice, troubleshooting, and unanswered questions. Apple hasn't said whether that archive will remain accessible after the closure. The Register asked Apple for the reasoning behind the termination. The company has yet to respond. ®

item.title: Meagan Good & Jonathan Majors Look Picture-Perfect at AFRIFF in Lagos
item.description: Meagan Good and Jonathan Majors coordinating in neutral tones and a red cap accent for AFRIFF. Who knew an ivory mini dress and a classic black suit could make such an interesting pairing? During their time in Lagos for AFRIFF, Meagan Good and Jonathan Majors posed for a studio portrait in two looks that took very different approaches to dressing up. Meagan’s dress brought together colourful beadwork, a fitted silhouette and a floor-length train, while Jonathan opted for black tailoring, an open-neck white shirt and a red cap. And while his outfit keeps things relatively simple, there’s nothing ordinary about the details of hers. Let’s start with Meagan’s dress, because there is quite a lot happening here. At first glance, the ivory mini might seem relatively simple, but look a little closer and the details begin to unfold. The fitted halter-neck bodice is covered in rows of turquoise, bronze and dark green beads, arranged horizontally to follow the shape of her waist. Then there’s the skirt, which takes a more unexpected turn with clusters of dark beaded embellishments scattered across the fabric. And just when you think you’ve taken it all in, an extended panel falls from the side of the mini skirt, creating a long, floor-sweeping train. It’s a fun combination of short and dramatic, with the beadwork giving the dress plenty to say without needing much else. Meagan Good styled in a sculpted halter-neck corset dress featuring multi-coloured beaded detailing and a side train. Meagan kept the rest of her styling fairly simple. Black ankle-strap heels and a textured black clutch were her accessories of choice, while her voluminous curls were left loose around her shoulders. Her bronze-toned makeup and glossy nude lip tied everything together without competing with the dress. Jonathan went in a completely different direction, keeping things classic with a black jacket and matching trousers over a white shirt, worn open at the neck. A grey patterned scarf added another detail around the collar, while his light-framed sunglasses and black patent shoes completed the outfit. But it’s the red cap that really changes the look. Against all that black and white, it gives the outfit a welcome hit of colour and makes the styling feel more personal. Meagan Good and Jonathan Majors showcasing intricate beaded dress embroidery and red cap styling. It’s an interesting pairing: Meagan’s dress has all the beadwork, colour and movement, while Jonathan’s outfit is built around simple tailoring and a few well-chosen accessories. There’s plenty to appreciate in both, wouldn’t you agree? Meagan Good displaying horizontal beadwork in turquoise and bronze paired with bronze-toned makeup. *** Photo Credit: Amplify Africa/Instagram The post Meagan Good & Jonathan Majors Look Picture-Perfect at AFRIFF in Lagos appeared first on BellaNaija - Showcasing Africa to the world. Read today! .

item.title: Shipping giant Maersk probes 'IT security incident,' data theft
item.description: Shipping behemoth A.P. Moller-Maersk says it is investigating "an IT security incident" involving the potential theft of data from a legacy system. In a statement issued on Wednesday, the Denmark-based shipping, cargo, and logistics giant confirmed it immediately launched an investigation into the attack and the affected system was secured. "Our findings so far strongly suggest no sensitive data has been disclosed," the company said . "The incident is isolated to a local system, and we have found no indication that there has been any impact on other Maersk systems or customer and partner systems that connect to Maersk through integrations such as APIs and EDI." Maersk described the legacy local system as one "from a previous acquisition," and said it does not expect the attack to have an effect on operations. Customers were reassured that they can continue to use Maersk platforms to manage their shipments as usual, and to expect updates from the company as and when they're available. "Cybersecurity remains a constant, ongoing priority for Maersk," it added. "We have rigorous processes in place to identify and prevent incidents and minimize customer impact. "As always, please treat any unexpected communications claiming to relate to this matter with caution and verify them through your usual Maersk contact. "Thank you for your patience as we continue to investigate the incident." Fortunately for those who immediately feel uneasy after hearing "Maersk" and "IT security" mentioned in the same breath, the wording of the shipping giant's disclosure suggests this intrusion won't be as calamitous as the NotPetya disaster in 2017. Mimicking the Petya ransomware strain, NotPetya was an infamous destructive wiper malware strain that wormed its way across the global economy. Western intelligence agencies attributed the malware to Russia's Sandworm group, an outfit believed to be part of the country's military intelligence service (GRU). Maersk said at the time that it expected the attack to result in a circa $300 million bill , owing to remediation and rebuild costs. Offering a sense of scale, Jim Hagemann Snabe, then chair of Maersk, told World Economic Forum delegates in 2018 that the company's rebuild encompassed 4,000 new servers, 45,000 new PCs, and 2,500 applications – which he said had been completed over just ten days. In 2020, as exclusively revealed by The Register , Maersk went on to lay off around 150 staffers from its command and control center in Maidenhead, England. The staffers who lost their jobs had played key roles in the recovery. ®

item.title: Google gooses Python AI performance by... removing Python
item.description: "Train in Python, serve in C++" might as well be Google's motto when it comes to much of its ML work. Python is easy for data scientists to wield, but keeping its interpreter in the serving pipeline can add overhead and deployment headaches. The industry-backed OpenXLA Project provides tools for compiling machine learning computations into native code for different processors. The latest component of this setup to be open sourced is XSE , short for the XLA Serving Engine. One-shot inference XSE is not so much suited for large-scale LLM inference (which would be better served by vLLM or SGLang ), but rather for smaller, more sharply task-oriented models, of which there are plenty at Google. "LLM serving gets most of the attention right now, but a significant amount of production inference is still ranking, recommendation, embedding, and vision models. These tend to be short requests with very high [queries-per-second] and tight latency budgets," Nathan Beach , Google director of product management, wrote in a LinkedIn missive Tuesday. At Google, XSE already handles more than six million queries per second across services including YouTube Shorts, Google Ads, and Search. These models aren't there for a leisurely chat. They rank results, recommend videos, and make other decisions on the fly, often without users noticing. A Python interpreter mulling each request would be a bottleneck, if not the end of Google itself. In Google's tests on short requests, XSE delivered two to five times the throughput of its best optimized Python server, using a quarter of the memory. No Python here In this setup, the ML boffins write their model code in Python, using Google's JAX to help with the sums. Google also plans integration with TorchTPU so PyTorch users can export models for C++ serving on TPUs. An export tool packages the model's computations in StableHLO, a portable intermediate representation, alongside its trained weights in an "XLA SavedModel." Ready to precognate, the C++ serving runtime uses XLA to compile those computations into native code for the target silicon. No Python interpreter to see here. XLA SavedModels can run on GPUs and CPUs – Google partnered with both Arm and Intel to develop the XLA ecosystem. But Google obviously thinks it'd be a lot cooler if you ran your models on its own line of TPU accelerators . Python's sluggishness continues to be an issue for the ML community. Beyond XSE, other approaches have been taken, many of which involve jettisoning the Python code as quickly as possible. PyTorch offers a native C++ runtime called LibTorch . Also, Microsoft and its collaborators offer the ONNX Runtime , which supports an open graph format with Python bindings. Even Python's own reference implementation relies heavily on C, with Rust now getting a foot in the door. ®

item.title: What Are The Effective Ways of Using AI?
item.description: Two people engaging with technology in a contemporary hotel lobby work setting. Artificial Intelligence (AI) is changing how people learn, work, communicate and solve problems. In today’s world, if you’re not on board with AI, it could be said you’re being resistant to the fastest-growing technological innovation in the world. From students researching academic subjects to professionals developing business ideas, AI tools have become companions in everyday activities for people. They can help save time, explore new ideas, understand difficult concepts and approach tasks differently. However, as more people embrace these AI tools, it is important to understand that using AI effectively goes beyond knowing what prompts to enter. It requires knowing when to use it, how to question its responses and, most importantly, when to rely on your own knowledge and judgement. AI could make us better at what we do, not make us dependent on it. Here are ways we think you use AI effectively: Use AI as a Research Assistant One of the most effective ways to use AI is for research and information gathering. Whether you are writing an article, preparing a presentation or exploring an unfamiliar subject, AI can help you identify relevant topics, explain complex ideas and suggest areas worth investigating. You can ask it to break down unfamiliar concepts, identify key questions, or suggest research directions. However, do not treat every response as fact. Verify important information using credible sources, published research, books and reliable websites. AI can help you find information, but you are responsible for establishing what is true. Use AI to Brainstorm and Explore Ideas Like knowledge gathering, AI can brainstorm ideas with you. Sometimes, the hardest part of starting a project is knowing where to begin. AI can help you overcome this challenge by suggesting ideas, exploring different approaches and presenting perspectives you may not have considered. For writers, entrepreneurs, researchers and creatives, it can be a useful brainstorming partner. You can share an idea, ask questions about its strengths and weaknesses, and explore ways to develop it. However, brainstorming should not become an excuse to surrender your imagination. Let AI expand your thinking, not replace it. Use AI to Improve Your Work, Not Replace Your Skills This is becoming more important. AI can help you identify grammatical errors, improve sentence construction, organise information, summarise lengthy documents and make your communication clearer. It can reduce the time spent on repetitive tasks and create more room for important responsibilities. The important thing is that you should remain actively involved. Read what AI produces, question its suggestions and make the final decisions yourself. Your skills improve when you practise them, not when you consistently hand them over to a machine. item.title: From Lagos to Cotonou! BN’s Osas is Taking You Inside SIMA 2026
item.description: One thing you can always bet on, as far as BellaNaija is concerned, is our alignment with African culture, creativity, and the people shaping the continent’s stories. “For where our treasure is, our heart will be”. And this time around, our heart is in Cotonou! Oh, and so are we! Hey BNers! Osas Okonyon here, and I’m heading to the Republic of Benin for the third edition of the Salon des Industries Musicales d’Afrique Francophone (SIMA), where I’ll be over the next few days. SIMA is bringing together artists, music executives, producers, creatives, investors and other key players in the African music industry for conversations about the future of our sound, the business behind it, and how African music can continue to make its mark on the world. This year’s theme, “African Music: From the Stage to Global Influence,” is particularly exciting. Beyond the music we love and the artists we celebrate, there’s so much to explore about the business, opportunities, collaborations and structures that help African creativity thrive. From conversations around music financing, artificial intelligence and intellectual property to the intersections of music, fashion, film, tourism and sports, SIMA promises a fascinating look into the evolving creative landscape. So, whether you’re a music lover, a creative, an industry enthusiast or simply someone who loves experiencing Africa through its people and culture, come along with me. I’ll be bringing you the conversations, the discoveries, the behind-the-scenes moments and, of course, all the good vibes from Cotonou. Put on your seatbelts, BNers. We’re about to get into the sound and influence of African music! item.description:
Tariq is the Editor-in-Chief of Space.com based out of our New York City office and joined the team in 2001, first as an intern and staff writer, and later as an editor. He covers human spaceflight, exploration and space science, as well as skywatching and entertainment. He became Space.com's Managing Editor in 2009 and Editor-in-Chief in 2019. In October 2022, Tariq received the Harry Kolcum Award for excellence in space reporting from the National Space Club Florida Committee. In June 2025, the National Space Society awarded him the Space Pioneer Award for Excellence in Mass Media at the International Space Development Conference in Orlando, Florida.

Hailing from Stockton, California (where he attended the same high school as NASA astronaut Jose Hernandez), Tariq studied print journalism and astronomy at the University of Southern California in Los Angeles, earning a bachelor's degree in journalism in 1999 along with a minor in astronomy. He then served as a staff reporter for The Los Angeles Times covering education and city beats in La Habra and Fullerton in Orange County for the Our Times sections.

In 2000, Tariq became the city reporter for the Huntington Beach Independent, a weekly publication of the Los Angeles Times, covering local politics and events, crime, business and environmental issues. He left the Los Angeles Times in 2001 to study science journalism at New York University, where he earned a master's degree in 2002 from NYU's Science and Environmental Reporting Program (now the Science, Health and Environmental Reporting Program) under the direction of space reporter William Burrows.

Tariq first joined Space.com as an intern in September 2001 while also serving as a research assistant for nutrition writer Gary Taubes and writing freelance projects, where his work appeared in The Scientist and Laboratory Equipment Magazine. He became a full-time reporter covering spaceflight in 2004, with this first launch being NASA's STS-114 Return to Flight mission in July 2005.

Tariq is also an Eagle Scout (yes, he has the Space Exploration merit badge) and went to Space Camp four times as a kid and a fifth time as an adult. When not writing about space, you can find Tariq watching the latest Star Trek TV series, sci-fi movies and reading about hippos, his favorite animal. You can find Tariq at Space.com and as the co-host to the This Week In Space podcast with space historian Rod Pyle on the TWiT network. To see his latest project, you can follow Tariq on Twitter @tariqjmalik.

item.title: Linux joins Heathrow's grounded fleet of information screens
item.description: UK travelers had more than fog to contend with this week, as Linux proved that if Windows could bork anything, it could bork it better. Spotted by Andy Hinks at Heathrow Airport's Terminal 2, this information display has seen better days. While its neighbors offer walking times and terminal maps, it presents a sideways Linux boot log – useful only if your next connection involves mounting a filesystem. There aren't many clues to what has befallen the machine behind the screen. The boot messages mention systemd , an Intel PRO/1000 network adapter, and an EXT4 filesystem on what appears to be a logical volume named LV_ROOT . Whether mounting that filesystem is the problem, or simply the last thing displayed before something else went wrong, isn't clear. Heathrow's information displays clearly accommodate a mixture of technologies. Recent examples ran Microsoft Windows, which had - naturally - suffered a moment of its own. Linux can evidently be just as unreliable in the right hands. The question is which Linux distribution is having its moment in the sun. Heathrow has been rolling out Raspberry Pi-based signage, although the Intel PRO/1000 adapter leaves the hardware behind this particular display something of a mystery. Pi hardware makes sense for signage: it's relatively cheap – at least until AI ate all the RAM – and low-powered compared with a full-fat Windows PC. Heathrow's senior product owner for displays described the approach as a "reliable, secure solution that has a significantly lower hardware cost and are 30-40% more energy efficient than our previous hardware." Readers might be interested to know that Heathrow has spent years working on its new screens. The product owner again: "We've completely re-engineered our content distribution system to be flexible and device-agnostic." So Windows in one place, and Linux somewhere else. All rubbing along famously. Assuming, of course, the displays can show more than a virtual cough and splutter during boot. ®

item.title: AMD: Where we're going we don't need (as much) DRAM
item.description: AMD's latest sales pitch: Up to 99 percent of the performance with half the DRAM, provided you're willing to buy a Mext license alongside your shiny new Epyc server. This is made possible by using AI models to load memory pages in and out of cheaper NVMe storage before your operating system or apps ever know they need it — kind of like SWAP or a Windows page file, but smarter. AMD acquired the tech from Mext back in June, and according to former CEO Gary Smerdon — now CVP of business development at AMD — the tech could cut enterprise server costs by as much as 83 percent by replacing costly RDIMMs with flash storage. Of the initial 145 systems the software has been deployed on so far, he estimates customers have already saved $5 million in avoided DRAM costs. "Conservatively, 60, 70, even 80 or 90 percent for very large memory systems, of the cost of a server can be in memory," he explained. Everyone's favorite buzzword to the rescue Even in systems with high memory utilization, where (say) 95 percent of the memory is "in use," a lot of it isn't actively being used, he explained. He cited a Meta research paper that showed that between 50 and 80 percent of memory pages hadn't been touched in five minutes, ten minutes, or even longer. "Five minutes to Epyc is an eternity." Mext technology aims to offload those infrequently accessed pages to flash. The challenge, Smerdon explains, is that while flash may be 50x cheaper per bit, 30x lower power per bit, it's also 500x slower. This is why most folks, when provisioning VPCs or servers, generally avoid swapping out to disk wherever possible: it kills application performance and sends service level agreements out the window. So for Mext's tech to work, it needed to ensure that any pages offloaded to storage were back in DRAM before they're needed. Kind of like running an errand in the middle of the workday – so long as you're back before your boss needs you again, they'll never know you left your desk. The problem was that the "R" in DRAM stands for random. Predicting which pages the system was going to need at which time isn't exactly trivial. The solution? (Brace for it.) "We realized we could use AI to monitor the system and proactively push those pages back into DRAM, so that as far as the application or the operating system knew, they were there the whole time," Smerdon said. In other words: "We transparently make flash appear as DRAM." So, "instead of buying two terabytes of DRAM for your Epyc-based server, you could buy one terabyte of DRAM, and then the next terabyte comes with Mext." To do this, AMD’s Mext employs a number of machine learning algorithms. "The workhorse model is a transformer derivative model, just like ChatGPT or Claude or the other famous models, but instead of predicting, for example, in the case of text, what word is next, what we're doing is predicting what page of memory is going to be required next," Smerdon explained. item.title: Forget the Usual Black Suit, Priscilla Ojo Is Making a Case for Chocolate Brown
item.description: Priscilla Ojo wearing an embellished chocolate brown suit co-ord paired with pointed-toe camel pumps Who says a business launch calls for the usual power suit? Priscilla Ojo had a different idea when she stepped out to introduce her latest venture, PalmPriy. The content creator, entrepreneur and style tastemaker chose a rich chocolate brown two-piece, but this was no ordinary office suit. With bronze and amber beaded fringe running across the jacket, her look brought a little extra personality to corporate dressing. The suit makes a case for giving brown tailoring a place in your wardrobe. Its single-breasted blazer features sharp shoulders and a defined waist, while the floor-length wide-leg trousers give the outfit a relaxed, fluid finish. Then come the embellishments: heavy bronze and amber beads tracing the lapels, hemline and cuffs. They add movement and texture to the jacket, making it the piece that draws the eye without overwhelming the overall look. Priscilla Ojo styled in a custom beaded chocolate brown suit for the official launch of her business, PalmPriy. Priscilla also got the proportions right with her footwear. She paired the wide-leg trousers with pointed-toe camel pumps, allowing just a glimpse of the shoes beneath the long hems. The rest of her accessories stayed simple, with subtle drop earrings and delicate rings leaving the embellished suit plenty of room to speak for itself. A detailed view of Priscilla Ojo’s chocolate brown blazer featuring hand-sewn pearls and beaded fringe. Her beauty look followed the warm colour palette. She wore her hair in long, cascading waves with copper highlights, parted down the middle, and completed the look with bronze-toned soft glam and a glossy nude lip. For anyone looking to take their tailoring beyond the familiar black or grey suit, Priscilla’s PalmPriy launch outfit offers a lovely starting point. Chocolate brown, wide-leg trousers and a little embellishment make for a combination worth considering, whether you’re dressing for a business event or looking to give your workwear a new direction. item.title: UK's 'buy British' tech ambitions hit reality as less than £1 in £6 stays at home
item.description: The UK government talks a good game about buying British, but less than £1 in every £6 spent with its biggest technology suppliers goes to British firms, according to research exposing how much Whitehall relies on foreign tech. A report from the Institute for Public Policy Research (IPPR) found that while 42.5 percent of spending with the public sector's 150 largest technology suppliers appears to go to UK companies, that figure collapses to just 15.4 percent once you look beyond where those businesses happen to be headquartered. A UK headquarters doesn't necessarily make a company British. Some are owned from overseas, others have most of their staff abroad, and many simply resell technology from US giants such as Microsoft. In fact, 43 percent of the spending attributed to UK-headquartered suppliers goes to resellers. Bytes and Softcat alone account for around £2 billion, making them two of the three biggest recipients of public sector technology spending. Once researchers traced reseller contracts back to the companies behind the products, the US emerged as the biggest beneficiary, accounting for £9.2 billion of the £19.2 billion spent with the largest suppliers. And the money isn't exactly being spread around. Just 150 companies receive 83 percent of public sector technology spending, with the largest 15 accounting for almost half. Smaller suppliers aren't getting much of a look-in either, receiving just 12 percent of government technology spending compared with 27 percent of spending across government as a whole. Competition is another concern. According to IPPR, 89.9 percent of government IT contracts over the past 12 months had no published record of how many suppliers bid for the work, making it difficult to assess how competitive those procurements were. Things get murkier when AI enters the picture, naturally. Government spending records show relatively little money going directly to the likes of OpenAI and Anthropic, but that doesn't mean Whitehall isn't buying their technology. Much of it is bundled into existing cloud agreements, enterprise software licenses, and partnerships. One example is NHS England's rollout of Microsoft 365 Copilot to 505,000 staff , which IPPR says was carried out under a national licensing agreement signed in June 2023, before Copilot was even generally available. That means AI tools can reach hundreds of thousands of public sector workers through deals negotiated before those products were on the market, potentially leaving rival suppliers without an opportunity to compete. The report, Locked In: A Realist's Agenda for Digital Sovereignty, warns that Britain's dependence on American technology could become particularly troublesome if Washington restricts access to advanced AI systems. It points to recent US restrictions on Anthropic models and limits on early access for Britain's AI Security Institute as evidence that such concerns are no longer entirely hypothetical. item.title: OpenAI builds a kill switch for its research models
item.description: In 2019, OpenAI decided not to publicly release a new model because its research uncovered “concerns about malicious applications of the technology.” And on Tuesday, the company announced it has built a kill switch for the models deployed in its research labs, months after some of them displayed disturbing behavior. “As our models get more powerful and the associated safety and security risks become bigger, it becomes more and more critical that we can detect potential issues, and quickly stop models in their tracks when needed,” OpenAI explains in a Tuesday post . The company named the kill switch “Control Room” and described it as “a central system to track model workloads across our research infrastructure and stop them quickly when safety or security concerns arise.” The facility can apparently stop models from producing any output 35 seconds after a decision to pull the plug – and can go faster. “The 35-second lag comes from a caching layer for inference authorization, to support the required volume of traffic. We are working to drive this number down to zero so that we can end jobs instantly,” the company promises. A rookie mistake in critical infrastructure design is to build both production and resilience tools on shared resources that could be taken offline by a single incident. OpenAI seems conscious of that risk, because it says the tool “has been built to keep working even when other systems fail, and to stop model output if Control Room itself goes down.” OpenAI hasn’t explained why it took so long to build a kill switch or why it decided now is the moment when it needs one. The Register fancies recent examples of agents exceeding their brief in worrying ways – like attacking Hugging Face , causing trouble at the Wikimedia Foundation , or going a little too deep when researching Australian healthcare data – may have influenced the timing of this development. “Control Room is already deployed across our research infrastructure, where the need is greatest,” the company’s announcement states. “Our external model-serving stack is already much more centralized by nature, with a well-developed operational capability to quickly take down model deployments if needed.” OpenAI says it plans to “strengthen and expand the system over the coming months, alongside our investments in monitoring for misaligned behavior and security breaches.” That’s a variant of Big Tech’s usual “We’re sorry and we promise to do better in future” proclamation that follows the latest SNAFU. Yet back in 2019, OpenAI pulled the pin before matters ever reached that state. ®

item.title: APOD: 2026 November 11 – NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact
item.description: APOD Science APOD APOD: 2026 November 11 – NGC… Today’s APOD Archive Submissions Index Search Calendar RSS Education About Discuss APOD Astronomy Picture of the Day Discover the cosmos! Each day a different image or photograph of our fascinating universe is featured, along with a brief explanation written by a professional astronomer. NGC 4449: Small Galaxy, Big Impact Explanation: Don’t judge a galaxy by its size. Our home galaxy, the Milky Way , is about 100,000 light years across. This huge expanse of space contains hundreds of billions of stars! The smallest galaxies, called dwarf galaxies , are about 1/10th the size of the Milky Way and only contain a few billion stars. They are also the most common type of galaxy in the whole universe. Today’s image shows one such dwarf galaxy, NGC 4449 , captured by the Hubble Space Telescope . NGC 4449 and similar dwarf galaxies are missing more oxygen than models predict. This suggests their stellar winds and supernovae are surprisingly effective at blowing away oxygen and other heavy elements. Turns out these tiny galaxies may play a big role in spreading heavy elements — the building blocks of stars, planets, and life — throughout the universe! item.title: Water Surges Into Navajo Reservoir
item.description: Earth Observatory Science Earth Observatory Water Surges Into Navajo… Earth Earth Observatory Image of the Day EO Explorer Topics All Topics Atmosphere Land Heat & Radiation Life on Earth Human Dimensions Natural Events Oceans Remote Sensing Technology Snow & Ice Water More Content Collections Global Maps World of Change Articles Earth Matters Blog Blue Marble: Next Generation EO Kids Mission: Biomes About About Us Subscribe 🛜 RSS Contact Us Search September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison NASA Earth Observatory/Michala Garrison September 20, 2026 November 7, 2026 Curtain Toggle 2-Up Back-to-back extreme rain events inundated the Four Corners region of the U.S. Southwest in late October and early November 2026. The storms alleviated short-term drought conditions in the Southwest but caused river levels to spike to record or near-record levels in places, triggering damaging floods. One effect of the heavy rains detected by satellites was the rapid rise of water levels in Navajo Reservoir. The change is visible in the images above, acquired on September 20 (left) and November 7 (right) with the OLI (Operational Land Imager) on Landsat 9 . In that time, the lake in northern New Mexico and southern Colorado rose by nearly 60 feet (18 meters), according to data from the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers. (Note that the Bureau of Reclamation decreased releases from Navajo Dam on September 16 and 17.) On November 7, the reservoir stood at its highest level since August 2019 and at 108 percent of the average capacity for that date. That contrasts with September 20, when it held just 60 percent of its average capacity. Due to snow drought across the West in winter 2025-26, the lake saw relatively little growth in the spring, when snowmelt often raises water levels. The San Juan, Piedra, and other rivers swelled with runoff amid the wet weather. Pagosa Springs, Colorado, a town along the San Juan River about 40 miles (64 kilometers) northeast of the lake, was especially hard-hit by flooding. In the first round of rain, 5.05 inches (12.8 centimeters) fell in the town, and on October 23 the river reached major flood stage . After more rain, the river spiked again on November 1, this time nearly to the record level set in 1911 during a devastating flood . Officials issued evacuation orders, and responders rescued dozens of people, according to news reports , while water inundated streets and damaged property. Heavy rain and flooding have been widespread across southwest Colorado, southeast Utah, northern Arizona, and northwest New Mexico in recent weeks. From early September through early November, precipitation totals were 2 to 4 times the average throughout the Four Corners region—an area beset by long-term drought that was exacerbated by snow drought and high temperatures in 2026. item.title: Australia may make knowingly selling unsafe AI a crime
item.description: Australia’s government will consider creating a new criminal offense to punish AI companies which knowingly release harmful models. Canberra dangled that possibility yesterday when releasing the results of an investigation into OpenAI’s admission that its agents accessed non-public medical records – and that it didn’t disclose the incident for weeks. Security at the agency which held those records fell short of contemporary best practice but Canberra nonetheless ordered a rapid review into Australia’s ability to handle infosec incidents involving AI. That review landed yesterday, complete with 18 recommendations including one that would make it mandatory for AI companies to report misaligned behavior or security incidents involving their models, and perhaps impose criminal penalties for “egregious regulatory non-compliance.” Another recommendation calls for consideration of “A standalone ‘failure to prevent’ offence which would criminalize instances where the company is responsible for developing an AI model that engages in harmful conduct, and the company fails to take reasonable steps to prevent that harm.” The review suggests two ministries and Australia’s Federal Police consider those reforms, meaning this is not something that will happen in a hurry, if at all, for a couple of reasons. One is that Australia yesterday proposed a new regulator which will require AI players to do six things: Maintain security controls across all stages of development and deployment Identify and manage serious risks associated with their models Allow independent evaluation of their models Provide mandatory notification of incidents to the Australian Government rapidly Maintain and publish safety and security frameworks to ensure good governance, risk management and transparency Respond to updated standards and rules as technologies change. If AI companies straighten up and fly right, Canberra might not need to do more. The other reason Australia might not criminalize AI is economic pragmatism. Canberra wants to ensure leading AI companies invest in local datacenters, especially facilities where they train and run frontier models. Such investments would mean Australia scores some of the AI boom cash sloshing around the world, while also giving the government the ability to at least point to leading-edge AI running on local shores and therefore theoretically remaining accessible even if war or a diplomatic rupture makes it hard to access advanced AI hosted offshore. Other nations in Asia, such as South Korea and India, are addressing those risks by building substantial sovereign infrastructure and working to develop sovereign frontier-class models trained on local data and especially data in their local languages. Canberra can’t match that investment without pouring petrol on its raging inflation problem. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese is therefore instead trying to regulate AI without scaring away investment. Threatening to lock up AI executives is not likely to

item.title: Anthropic tiptoes into MS Office territory
item.description: Anthropic has introduced three new types of artifacts that show the company tiptoeing into the office productivity market long dominated by Microsoft and Google. On Tuesday, the Claudefather announced Claude Sheets, Claude Whiteboards, and Claude Data, and promised the imminent arrival of Claude Meetings. These artifact types join existing ones – Docs, Slides, Design, and Motion – to form a nascent Claude-dependent productivity suite. Anthropic initially used the term artifacts to refer to shareable AI-based interactive tools, like dynamic charts. But the scope of the term has been stretched to cover specific artifact types, which refer to what traditionalists might take to mean files associated with specific hosted applications. "An artifact is anything Claude makes for you that you'd put in front of someone: a design, a deck, a document, a dashboard, or a small interactive tool," the company explains. The key thing that distinguishes an artifact from a file is that users are meant to interact with artifacts through Claude, rather than storing and transferring them independently. Think of it more as a container or managed object that opens in Claude (via a sharing URL), because artifacts in fact consist of various content types – .txt, .md, .html, .jsx, .svg, .pptx, .docx, .zip, .pdf, and .mp4, among others. Anthropic's vision of Claude as a container for other applications goes beyond artifacts. The AI biz has also expanded its interactive connectors , which turn Claude into a landlord for other software applications. Its own promotional video for the feature hammers that point home in its title: " Your apps have moved into Claude ." "Starting today, partners can embed their apps directly in Claude, so you can work in Adobe, Atlassian, and others without switching tabs," Anthropic said. "Plugins from Salesforce (beta), NetSuite, and Workday (beta) come with built-in skills, so sellers can prep for a call, accountants can analyze financial data, and HR teams can handle time off and expenses." In a prior era, those would be fighting words. Tech companies like Apple, Google, and Microsoft have worked for years to maintain their positions as platform landlords. Anthropic's invitation to become a Claude tenant ought to set off competition alarm bells. But perhaps with LLMs being able to re-create other people's apps on demand, there's less interest in defending app boundaries as if they were moats to keep out rivals. With AI, the call is coming from inside the house. Alongside the rollout of Claude Sheets, Whiteboards, and Data, Anthropic is pushing the notion that Claude is useful for people working outside of computation and mathematics, the occupational category that, according to the company's own data , accounts for a larger share of Claude usage than any other. "Inside Anthropic, non-technical teams are starting to get as much out of Claude as our engineers," the biz insists, hauling out canned testimonials from the likes of Accenture and Data

item.title: Seagate's new hybrid drive raises some old questions
item.description: Seagate doesn't think hybrid drives are done just yet. On Tuesday, the company announced the launch of the new FireCuda Forge line of storage drives. The new drives combine the high capacity of a traditional plattered HDD with the speed and responsiveness of a user-supplied solid-state drive (SSD). The new hybrid storage solution is Seagate's first to be powered and managed by the new Alkemi intelligent storage platform. The FireCuda Forge is available right now through Seagate's web store , and comes in 8TB ($699) or 20TB ($899) HDD configurations—neither of which includes the required SSD. Users will have to bring their own SSD, with some specific restrictions. The FireCuda Forge is compatible with M.2 2280 NVMe drives that are PCIe Gen3 or higher. The maximum supported NVMe capacity is 1TB, which means that's as much data as you'll be able to dedicate to storage on the "fast side" of the hybrid setup. The NVMe will require minimum speeds of 2,400MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write, and a unit with DRAM cache is recommended. Seagate claims 2,500MB/s read and 2,000MB/s write speeds for the combined system, along with USB4 and support for Windows 11 and macOS 26+. Credit: Seagate Read full article Comments
